#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Construction (SOC)
Description: The Survey of Construction (SOC) provides national and regional statistics on starts and completions of new single-family and multifamily housing units and statistics on sales of new single-family houses in the United States. The SOC also provides statistics on characteristics of new privately-owned residential structures in the United States. Data included are various characteristics of new single-family houses completed, new multifamily housing completed, new single-family houses sold, and new contractor-built houses started. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) partially funds this survey.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

[Federal Register Volume 91, Number 137 (Monday, July 20, 2026)]
[Notices]
[Pages 45237-45238]
From the Federal Register Online via the Government Publishing Office [www.gpo.gov]
[FR Doc No: 2026-14512]


-----------------------------------------------------------------------

DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE

Census Bureau


Agency Information Collection Activities; Submission to the 
Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for Review and Approval; Comment 
Request; Survey of Housing Starts, Sales, and Completions

AGENCY: Census Bureau, Department of Commerce.

ACTION: Notice of information collection, request for comment.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Department of Commerce, in accordance with the Paperwork 
Reduction Act (PRA) of 1995, invites the general public and other 
Federal agencies to comment on proposed, and continuing information 
collections, which helps us assess the impact of our information 
collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting burden. The 
purpose of this notice is to allow for 60 days of public comment on the 
proposed extension of the Survey of Housing Starts, Sales, and 
Completions, prior to the submission of the information collection 
request (ICR) to OMB for approval.

DATES: To ensure consideration, comments regarding this proposed 
information collection must be received on or before September 18, 
2026.

ADDRESSES: Interested persons are invited to submit written comments by 
email to [email protected]. Please reference Survey of Housing 
Starts, Sales, and Completions in the subject line of your comments. 
You may also submit comments, identified by Docket Number USBC-2026-
0298, to the Federal e-Rulemaking Portal: http://www.regulations.gov. 
All comments received are part of the public record. No comments will 
be posted to http://www.regulations.gov for public viewing until after 
the comment period has closed. Comments will generally be posted 
without change. All Personally Identifiable Information (for example, 
name and address) voluntarily submitted by the commenter may be 
publicly accessible. Do not submit Confidential Business Information or 
otherwise sensitive or protected information. You may submit 
attachments to electronic comments in Microsoft Word, Excel, or Adobe 
PDF file formats.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Requests for additional information or 
specific questions related to collection activities should be directed 
William Abriatis, U.S. Census Bureau, Economic Indicators Division, 
(301) 763-3686, or [email protected].

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Abstract

    The U.S. Census Bureau plans to request a three-year extension of 
the current Office of Management and Budget (OMB) clearance of the 
Survey of Housing Starts, Sales and Completions, also known as the 
Survey of Construction (SOC). The SOC is co-sponsored by the U.S. 
Census Bureau and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development 
(HUD). The SOC collects monthly data on new residential construction 
from a sample of owners or builders. The Census Bureau uses the 
Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI) electronic 
questionnaires SOC-QI/SF.1 and SOC-QI/MF.1 to collect data on start and 
completion dates of construction, physical characteristics of the 
structure (floor area, number of bathrooms, type of heating system, 
etc.), and if applicable, date of sale, sales price, and type of 
financing. The SOC provides widely used measures of construction 
activity, including the economic indicators Housing Starts and Housing 
Completions, which are from the New Residential Construction series, 
and New Residential Sales. The current clearance for this survey is 
scheduled to expire on March 31, 2027.
    We sample approximately 1,613 new buildings each month 
(approximately 19,353 per year). We inquire about the progress of each 
building multiple times until it is completed (and a sales contract is 
signed, if it is a single-family house that is built for sale). For 
single-family buildings, we conduct an average of 9.6 interviews and 
for multifamily buildings, we conduct an average of 8.5 interviews. The 
total number of interviews conducted from 2023 through 2025 was 
averaged and for single-family buildings is approximately 120,312 and 
for multifamily buildings is about 57,390. Each interview takes 5 
minutes on average. Therefore, the total annual burden is 14,809 hours. 
Compared to the period 2020-2022, sampled construction projects are 
taking longer to start, complete, and sell. Since projects are 
interviewed until the project is completed or sold for the single-
family for sale category, this is leaving projects in sample for longer 
resulting in a higher average interview amount for 2023-2025. While the 
amount of sampled projects has decreased, the average interviews per 
case increasing results in a modest increase in total annual burden for 
this collection.

II. Method of Collection

    The Census Bureau uses its field representatives to collect the 
data. The field representatives conduct interviews to obtain data.

III. Data

    OMB Control Number: 0607-0110.
    Form Number(s): SOC-QI.SF.1 and SOC-QI/MF.1.
    Type of Review: Regular submission, Request for an Extension, 
without Change, of a Currently Approved Collection.
    Affected Public: Individuals or households; Business or other for-
profit organizations.
    Estimated Number of Respondents: We sample 19,353 new buildings 
each year. This results in an estimated 177,702 interviews per year.
    Estimated Time per Response: 5 minutes.
    Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours: 14,809.

[[Page 45238]]

    Estimated Total Annual Cost to Public: $0. (This is not the cost of 
respondents' time, but the indirect costs respondents may incur for 
such things as purchases of specialized software or hardware needed to 
report, or expenditures for accounting or records maintenance services 
required specifically by the collection.)
    Respondent's Obligation: Voluntary.
    Legal Authority: Title 13, United States Code, Sections 8(b), 131 
and 182; Title 12 U.S.C., Sections 1701z-1 and 1701z-2g

IV. Request for Comments

    We are soliciting public comments to permit the Department/Bureau 
to: (a) Evaluate whether the proposed information collection is 
necessary for the proper functions of the Department, including whether 
the information will have practical utility; (b) Evaluate the accuracy 
of our estimate of the time and cost burden for this proposed 
collection, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions 
used; (c) Evaluate ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of 
the information to be collected; and (d) Minimize the reporting burden 
on those who are to respond, including the use of automated collection 
techniques or other forms of information technology.
    Comments that you submit in response to this notice are a matter of 
public record. We will include, or summarize, each comment in our 
request to OMB to approve this ICR. Before including your address, 
phone number, email address, or other personal identifying information 
in your comment, you should be aware that your entire comment--
including your personal identifying information--may be made publicly 
available at any time. While you may ask us in your comment to withhold 
your personal identifying information from public review, we cannot 
guarantee that we will be able to do so.

Sheleen Dumas,
Departmental PRA Compliance Officer, Office of the Under Secretary for 
Economic Affairs, Commerce Department.
[FR Doc. 2026-14512 Filed 7-17-26; 8:45 am]
BILLING CODE 3510-07-P

Overview of FY2026 Appropriations for the Census Bureau

September 2, 2025 – March 19, 2026 IF13105

Overview of FY2026 Appropriations for the Census Bureau
Updated March 19, 2026 (IF13105)

Introduction

As a Department of Commerce agency, the U.S. Census Bureau is primarily funded through the annual Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies (CJS) appropriations bill. This In Focus provides an overview of FY2026 appropriations for the U.S. Census Bureau; certain comparisons to previous years' appropriations; and congressional action to date. Information presented is drawn from the Census Bureau's FY2026 Congressional Budget Justification, the enacted FY2026 CJS bill, and other relevant congressional documents.

The FY2026 appropriations are divided between two accounts: Current Surveys and Programs, and Periodic Censuses and Programs. For these two accounts, comparisons are made here between the FY2026 enacted level, the FY2026 request, and enacted amounts for FY2024 and FY2025. (The FY2025 full-year continuing resolution [CR] funded these accounts in the same amounts and under the same authorities and conditions as enacted in FY2024.) The FY2026 budget justification also includes requested amounts below the account level in more detail, which are compared here to corresponding actual FY2024 amounts (the budget justification document does not provide this level of detail for FY2025 actual amounts).

Figure 1. Census Budget Authority

Source: Data from U.S. Census Bureau, FY2026 Congressional Budget Justification and FY2026 Appropriations.

Notes: Values may not add evenly due to rounding.

FY2026 Appropriations

The enacted FY2026 CJS bill (P.L. 119-74) includes $1.490 billion for the Census Bureau. This is $186 million less than the Trump Administration's FY2026 budget request of $1.677 billion and a $108 million increase from the FY2024 and FY2025 enacted levels of $1.383 billion.

Current Surveys and Programs

The bill includes $319 million for the Current Surveys and Programs account, which is $30 million above the Administration's FY2026 requested $289 million and a decrease of $10 million from the FY2024 and FY2025 enacted amounts of $329 million. This account includes funding for Current Economic Statistics and Current Demographic Statistics.

Current Economic Statistics

Current Economic Statistics include business, construction, manufacturing, general economic, foreign trade, and government statistics. According to the FY2026 budget justification, Current Economic Statistics programs "provide timely, accurate, and essential data on the structure and performance of the U.S. economy, supporting the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) estimation, fiscal and monetary policymaking, and private sector decision-making."

The FY2026 request for Current Economic Statistics was $216 million, the same as FY2024 and FY2025 actual amounts.

Current Demographic Statistics

Current Demographic Statistics includes the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP); the Current Population Survey (CPS), which is sponsored by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and the Census Bureau; and the Population Estimates Program. The SIPP is an ongoing survey that measures distribution of government assistance programs. The CPS provides estimates of income, poverty, and other indicators. The Population Estimates Program calculates population change over time. The Census Bureau's population estimates are used in a variety of federal programs to determine funding allocations or eligibility.

The FY2026 request for Current Demographic Statistics was $73 million, which is a $40 million decrease from FY2024 and FY2025 actual amounts of $113 million.

Proposed changes to these programs include testing internet self-response for the CPS and using some nonsurvey data to reduce costs for the SIPP.

Periodic Censuses and Programs

The bill includes $1.172 billion for the Periodic Censuses and Programs account, which is $216 million less than the Administration's FY2026 requested $1.388 billion and a $118 million increase from the FY2024 and FY2025 enacted amount of $1.054 billion. This account consists of funding for several programs discussed below.

Decennial Census

The FY2026 request for the decennial census account was $983 million, a $383 million increase from the FY2024 actual amount of $600 million. Requested FY2026 funding for the decennial census includes support for the 2026 Census Test and preparation for the 2028 Dress Rehearsal, full-scale development of core IT infrastructure, award and management of contracts, and continued data collection and publication for the American Community Survey (ACS). Unlike previous budget documents, the FY2026 budget justification does not specify the respective amounts for the 2030 decennial census and the ACS within the decennial census account.

Periodic Economic Statistics

The FY2026 request for the Periodic Economic Statistics Program, which contains the Economic Census and the Census of Governments, was $144 million, an $18 million decrease from the FY2024 actual level of $162 million. Specific funding levels for these two surveys are not provided in the FY2026 budget request.

The Economic Census, conducted every five years, collects statistics on businesses in the United States to help understand the U.S. economy. Requested FY2026 activities for the Economic Census include the continued review of 2022 Economic Census data releases.

The Census of Governments, conducted every five years, collects statistics on state and local governments across the United States. Requested FY2026 activities for the Census of Governments include the expanded use of administrative records and other data collection methods in preparation for the 2027 Census of Governments.

Geographic Support Program

The purpose of the Census Bureau's Geographic Support Program (GSP) is to support and maintain the geospatial infrastructure required to conduct survey data collection, processing, tabulation, and dissemination across covered regions. The Census Bureau considers the GSP to be foundational for all of its social and economic data products. Congressional district wall maps are produced by the GSP. The Census Bureau aims to utilize the GSP to minimize 2030 Census in-field enumeration costs.

The FY2026 request for the GSP was $98 million, a $14 million decrease from the FY2024 and FY2025 actual level of $112 million.

Enterprise Data Collection and Dissemination Systems (EDCaDS)

The EDCaDS generally supports the data collection, processing, and dissemination systems that are associated with Census Bureau programs.

The FY2026 request's stated goal for the EDCaDS is "to provide large cyclical systems that must be scaled for peak operations for the Decennial Census, the Economic Census, and the Census of Governments."

The FY2026 request for the EDCaDS was $163 million, a $17 million decrease from the FY2024 and FY2025 actual level of $180 million.

Congressional Action

The House Appropriations Committee CJS subcommittee marked up the House version of the FY2026 CJS appropriations bill on July 15, 2025. The bill, as approved by the subcommittee, would have provided $1.677 billion in total for the Census Bureau: $288.5 million for Current Surveys and Programs and $1.388 billion for Periodic Censuses and Programs. The bill, as reported, would have prohibited the Census Bureau from using any funds provided in the measure to include "aliens who are unlawfully present in the United States" in rendering apportionment determinations. It also included similar prohibitions on using any funds provided to enforce mandatory response requirements for certain Census Bureau surveys or to inquire more than twice to solicit voluntary survey responses. These provisions were not included in the version of the bill subsequently enacted into law. The bill advanced from the subcommittee by a 9-6 vote. The full committee ordered the bill reported by a 34-28 vote on September 10, 2025.

The Senate Appropriations Committee marked up its FY2026 CJS appropriations bill on July 17, 2025. The bill, as reported, would have provided $1.520 billion in total for the Census Bureau: $328.5 million for Current Surveys and Programs and $1.192 billion for Periodic Census and Programs. Furthermore, the committee report accompanying the bill directs the Census Bureau to provide information regarding the removal of Census and BEA data sets; the termination of Census Bureau advisory committees; ACS modernization efforts; 2030 decennial census operation plans; and the effects of field office closures. The report directs the Census Bureau to continue outreach to public libraries as partners for surveys and to prioritize carrying out the 2026 Census Test. The committee ordered the bill reported by a 19-10 vote.

Census Bureau appropriations lapsed from October 1 through November 12, 2025. The lapse ended when a CR providing appropriations for certain agencies (including the Commerce Department) through January 30, 2026, became law. The FY2026 CJS appropriations bill was included as part of a consolidated appropriations measure, which passed the House by a vote of 397-28 on January 8, 2026, and passed the Senate by a vote of 82-15 on January 15, 2026. The bill was signed into law by President Trump on January 23, 2026. The explanatory statement for the FY2026 CJS bill was filed in the Congressional Record by the chair of the House Appropriations Committee on January 8, 2026. The explanatory statement specifies that the Appropriations Committee reports accompanying the House and Senate versions of the FY2026 CJS appropriations bill carry "the same weight as language included in this joint explanatory statement and should be complied with unless specifically addressed to the contrary in this joint explanatory statement or in the act."

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Construction (SOC)
Description: The Survey of Construction (SOC) provides national and regional statistics on starts and completions of new single-family and multifamily housing units and statistics on sales of new single-family houses in the United States. The SOC also provides statistics on characteristics of new privately-owned residential structures in the United States. Data included are various characteristics of new single-family houses completed, new multifamily housing completed, new single-family houses sold, and new contractor-built houses started. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) partially funds this survey.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Research report: Survey of Construction (SOC)

**Research checked: October 9, 2026.** This report draws primarily on Census Bureau documentation, HUD’s dataset description, and federal information-collection notices. Recommendations for preservation and analysis are identified separately from documented program facts.

## Executive findings

**Your title and description are accurate.** Census describes the Survey of Construction in substantially the same terms, including HUD’s partial funding. However, several qualifications are essential:

- **The Census Bureau conducts and publishes the survey; HUD is a co-sponsor and partial funder.**
- **SOC is a survey program supporting multiple data products**, not one self-contained downloadable dataset.
- Its principal outputs include **New Residential Construction**, **New Residential Sales**, and **Characteristics of New Housing**.
- **Published SOC estimates principally cover the United States and four Census regions—not states, counties, or individual cities.**
- **Public-use microdata cover sampled single-family houses, not the full single-family and multifamily survey.**
- A new-home **“sale” means a signed contract or accepted deposit, not a completed closing**.
- **Survey participation is voluntary**, although collection is federally authorized and identifiable responses are legally protected.
- The data describe **new privately owned residential construction**, not the entire housing stock, all real-estate transactions, or net additions to housing supply. [1–5]

The dataset is especially valuable because it distinguishes **authorization, actual construction, completion, and sale**—events that administrative building-permit records alone cannot establish.

---

## 1. Identity, publisher, and institutional responsibility

| Field | Verified information |
|---|---|
| Official program name | Survey of Construction (SOC) |
| Alternative administrative title | Survey of Housing Starts, Sales, and Completions |
| Federal producer and publisher | U.S. Census Bureau, Department of Commerce |
| Sponsorship | Jointly sponsored by Census and the Department of Housing and Urban Development |
| HUD funding | Census explicitly states that HUD partially funds the survey |
| Operational responsibility | Census field representatives collect information; a 2026 federal notice identifies the Economic Indicators Division as the program contact |
| Main subject | New privately owned residential construction and sales of new single-family houses |
| Frequency | Monthly collection, with monthly, quarterly, and annual outputs |
| Core collection’s OMB control number | **0607-0110** |
| Related permit-office questionnaire | SOC-QBPO, OMB control number **0607-0125** |
| Public access | Free aggregate statistics, documentation, and disclosure-protected single-family microdata |

HUD’s website directs users to Census for the data and documentation. Thus, HUD’s catalog entry is useful for discovery and sponsorship information, but **Census is the authoritative distribution source**. [1,2,6,7]

### What should count as “the dataset”?

For cataloging or preservation, distinguish:

1. **The SOC survey program**—collection, sampling, questionnaires, and methodology.
2. **Aggregate statistical products** derived from SOC.
3. **Annual public-use microdata**.
4. **Related but separate collections**, especially the Building Permits Survey.

Treating all four as interchangeable would obscure provenance and produce analytical mistakes.

---

## 2. Legal authority, mandate, and confidentiality

### Collection authority

Census’s respondent letter identifies **13 U.S.C. §§131 and 182** as authority to conduct the collection and request voluntary assistance. [8]

The July 2026 Federal Register notice supplies a broader authority statement:

- **Title 13, §§8(b), 131, and 182**;
- **Title 12, §§1701z-1 and 1701z-2g**, as printed in the notice. [6]

These authorities connect Census’s statistical collection powers and interagency services with HUD’s housing research responsibilities.

**Important distinction:** SOC is an authorized federal statistical activity. That is not the same as a requirement that every selected builder respond. The official notice and respondent letter explicitly classify participation as **voluntary**. Nor do the sources reviewed establish that a SOC-specific statute permanently requires every current table or variable to be published.

### Paperwork Reduction Act oversight

The collection requires Office of Management and Budget approval under the **Paperwork Reduction Act**. The respondent letter states that Census cannot conduct the collection without that approval. [8]

The July 20, 2026 notice:

- proposed a **three-year extension without change**;
- stated that the existing clearance was scheduled to expire **March 31, 2027**;
- invited comments on utility, burden, data quality, clarity, and collection technology;
- identified docket **USBC-2026-0298**;
- set a comment deadline of **September 18, 2026**. [6]

The notice is evidence of an extension request—not proof that the proposed extension has subsequently been approved.

### Confidentiality

Under **13 U.S.C. §9**, Census must keep identifiable respondent information confidential and use responses to produce statistics. It cannot publicly release responses in a manner identifying the respondent business, organization, or institution. Census also cites the **Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2015** regarding screening of data-transmission systems. [1,8]

Public-use files remove identifying addresses and builders and modify certain potentially identifying values.

**Do not assume every associated record has the same confidentiality status.** Building permits are public records. The supporting statement for the separate SOC-QBPO collection also says that permit-office operating information is not confidential and receives no confidentiality assurance. [4,7]

---

## 3. What SOC measures—and what it excludes

### Principal products

| Product | Contents and purpose |
|---|---|
| **New Residential Construction (NRC)** | Housing units authorized but not started, started, under construction, and completed. The release also includes building-permit authorizations from the separate Building Permits Survey. |
| **New Residential Sales (NRS)** | New single-family houses sold and for sale; accompanying sales-price, inventory, and related market measures. |
| **Characteristics of New Housing** | Physical and financial characteristics of new single-family houses completed or sold, multifamily housing completed, and contractor-built houses started; some tables cover additional start-based categories. |
| **Annual SOC microdata** | Disclosure-protected records for sampled single-family houses and their construction/sales status. |

NRC and NRS are **Principal Federal Economic Indicators**. SOC’s website also links to construction price-index products, but their methods and intended uses should be cataloged separately. [1–4,9]

### Information collected

Documented examples include:

- construction start and completion dates;
- sale date;
- sales price, where applicable;
- floor area;
- bedrooms and bathrooms;
- heating-system characteristics;
- financing type;
- other physical and financial attributes.

The available variables and categories vary by product and year. A contemporary variable list should not be projected backward across the entire historical series. [1,3,6]

### Scope and exclusions

SOC/NRC statistics cover **privately owned new residential buildings**. They exclude:

- publicly owned housing;
- HUD-code manufactured/mobile homes;
- dormitories and other group quarters;
- transient hotels, motels, and similar accommodations;
- moved or relocated buildings;
- housing units created within existing residential or nonresidential structures.

Modular, panelized, sectional, and other qualifying factory-produced housing are not automatically excluded: **HUD-code manufactured homes and modular construction are different categories**.

Assisted-living units can qualify as housing units; nursing-home units do not. Residential units within new mixed-use buildings are included where possible.

Private construction with partial public subsidies can still count as privately owned construction. [5]

### New-home sales have a narrower universe

NRS includes qualifying **new single-family house-and-land sales**. It excludes:

- multifamily-unit sales;
- houses built for rent;
- owner-built houses;
- houses built by a general contractor on the owner’s land.

Those excluded homes may nevertheless be represented in construction statistics. **The starts universe and the sales universe are not identical.** [5]

---

## 4. Definitions that materially affect interpretation

| Term | Official meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Housing start** | Excavation begins for a building’s footings or foundation. All units in a multifamily building are counted as started at that point. | Starts are not permits, financing commitments, or apartment-by-apartment construction events. |
| **Completion: single-family** | Finished flooring is installed, or occupancy occurs before all construction is finished. | Completion does not necessarily mean every minor task is finished. |
| **Completion: multifamily** | All units in the building are counted when at least 50% are occupied or available for occupancy. | Large projects can enter the series as a batch. |
| **New house sold** | A sales contract is signed or a deposit accepted, potentially before construction or permit issuance. | Sales can lead construction and are not closings. |
| **New house for sale** | A qualifying built-for-sale house has a permit, or construction has begun in a nonpermit area, and no contract/deposit has been accepted. | This is not the entire real-estate listing inventory. |

Census does **not** follow the sales transaction through closing. A house remains counted as sold even if the initial transaction is not finalized. Beginning with September 1992 data, starts include structures totally rebuilt on an existing foundation. [5]

For historians and preservationists, this last provision is particularly important: the series is not a simple count of newly occupied parcels or wholly untouched sites.

---

## 5. History and changes over time

### Verified milestones

| Date | Significance |
|---|---|
| **1959** | Beginning of the published monthly and annual housing-starts series identified by Census |
| **1963** | Beginning of the new-home-sales series |
| **1968** | Beginning of the housing-completions series |
| **September 1992** | Starts definition expanded to include complete rebuilding on existing foundations |
| **1999** | Earliest currently listed annual public-use SOC microdata |
| **April 2001** | Revised estimation methodology implemented, with revisions back to January 1999 |
| **January 2005** | Beginning of the sample design described in Census’s methodology documentation |
| **2017 onward** | Public-use files display Census disclosure-review authorization numbers |
| **2020 onward** | Microdata distributed as unzipped XLSX rather than zipped XLS |
| **July 1, 2026** | Census reports publication of 2025 annual characteristics and microdata |

Sources: [1,3–5,10].

### Earlier historical context

The companion Building Permits Survey has older antecedents:

- USGS began federal building-permit-related collection in **1889**.
- BLS took over in **1920**, responding to post–World War I housing shortages.
- Building-permit estimation moved to Census in **1959**. [11]

**These are antecedents of the building-permit statistical system, not proof that SOC itself began in 1889 or 1920.** The earliest series dates should also not be mistaken for a fully documented institutional founding history.

### Comparability problems

Historical analysis must account for:

- changing definitions and questionnaires;
- sampling and estimation redesigns;
- variable additions and discontinuations;
- revised price ranges;
- late-response corrections;
- geographic-framework changes in related collections.

For example, Census revised 2014–2016 characteristics tables to incorporate previously omitted responses. It also recalculated and republished 2020–2022 sales-price groupings and related price statistics. Closing costs were last included in the statistics in 2007. [5,12]

The BPS changed its monthly design in 2022 and moved to an annually updated target universe in 2023. Because SOC estimation uses BPS totals, **BPS documentation is part of SOC’s analytical provenance**, even though the surveys are separate. [11,13]

---

## 6. Collection, sampling, and estimation

### Two components

SOC combines:

1. **Survey of Use of Permits (SUP):** follows sampled permits in places requiring building permits.
2. **Non-Permit Survey (NP):** identifies construction in sampled areas without permit requirements through field canvassing.

Census reports that less than 2% of new construction occurs in nonpermit areas. [4]

### Published sampling design

The methodology describes a three-stage design:

- selection of primary sampling units;
- selection of permit-issuing places and nonpermit land areas;
- monthly selection of permits or newly identified buildings.

The documented design includes approximately **900 permit-issuing places** and about **80 nonpermit land areas**. The general overview gives “more than 70” nonpermit areas, so these should be treated as approximate descriptions rather than an exact contemporaneous roster.

For buildings with one to four units, permits are sampled at an overall rate of about **1 in 50 units**. Permits for buildings with five or more units are all selected **within sampled permit offices**—not from every permit office nationwide. [1,4]

### Follow-up

Field representatives contact owners or builders, by telephone or in person, and collect responses using computer-assisted questionnaires. Selected buildings are followed until completion or abandonment; qualifying unsold single-family houses continue to be followed until sale. [1,6]

The 2026 burden estimate reports approximately:

- **1,613 newly sampled buildings monthly**;
- **19,353 annually**;
- **177,702 interviews annually**;
- five minutes per interview;
- **14,809 annual respondent hours**.

Average follow-up was estimated at 9.6 interviews per single-family building and 8.5 per multifamily building. These figures concern buildings and interviews, **not the number of housing units represented by the estimates**. [6]

### Estimation

Census applies sample weights and adjusts survey estimates using **Building Permits Survey authorization totals**, with adjustments by region, structure type, and permit timing.

Further adjustments address:

- starts occurring before permits are issued;
- prepermit sales;
- late reporting.

The current methodology makes **no adjustment for units built without permits in areas where permits are required**. This is distinct from construction in areas where permits are not required, which the NP component covers. [4]

---

## 7. Geography and representativeness

Standard SOC estimates are tabulated for:

- the United States;
- Northeast;
- Midwest;
- South;
- West.

Census expressly states that the sample is **not large enough for state or local-area estimates**.

Public-use microdata allow selected tabulations for the **nine Census divisions** and include an inside/outside-metropolitan-area indicator. They do not identify individual cities, counties, addresses, or builders. [3,4,14]

**Implications:**

- SOC is strong for national and broad regional trends.
- It is unsuitable by itself for evaluating one city’s zoning reform or neighborhood construction activity.
- Division-level cross-tabulations can become unstable when categories are narrow.
- For local authorizations, use BPS—but do not label permits as actual starts or completions.

---

### Microdata

Census currently lists annual files for **1999–2025**:

- **1999–2019:** zipped XLS;
- **2020 onward:** XLSX;
- SAS-format files are available by contacting the program.

Supporting resources include an Excel variable guide, a printer-friendly PDF guide, and a “Working with SOC Microdata” tutorial. The microdata page lists **301-763-5160** for SAS-format requests. [3]

### APIs

Aggregate economic-indicator series are available through Census’s Economic Indicator Time Series API:

- [`timeseries/eits/resconst`](https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/resconst.html)
- [`timeseries/eits/ressales`](https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/ressales.html)

The current developer documentation says **data queries require an API key**. Preserve variable metadata, geography metadata, and query parameters alongside returned JSON. The APIs should not be assumed to expose the annual house-level public-use files. [15]

### Rights and catalog metadata

The Data.gov record for the NRC API distribution identifies public access and a **CC0** license. That record’s metadata modification date is 2017 despite the ongoing time series—an instructive warning that **catalog timestamps are not observation dates or reliable indicators of current data freshness**. [16]

For a library catalog, record rights at the distribution level and distinguish public files from legally protected underlying responses.

---

## 9. Microdata: essential analytical cautions

Annual public-use files contain sampled single-family houses that were started, sold, and/or completed during the year, plus houses that remained:

- authorized but not started;
- under construction;
- for sale at year-end.

Abandoned projects are excluded. [3,14]

### Correct use

1. **Filter by the event of interest.**  
   The annual file is not simply “all houses completed that year.” Use start, sale, or completion dates and the appropriate construction-purpose category.

2. **Apply the sampling weight.**  
   `WEIGHT` indicates how many houses a sampled house represents. Unweighted record counts are sample counts, not national totals.

3. **Use the correct universe.**  
   Distinguish built-for-sale, contractor-built, owner-built, and built-for-rent houses.

4. **Expect imperfect agreement with published totals.**  
   Census says microdata tabulations will not exactly match published estimates, primarily because files and tables were produced at different times.

5. **Do not estimate total permit authorizations from these files.**  
   Census specifically warns that they do not provide accurate totals for all units authorized by permits. [14]

### Disclosure protection

The files omit specific addresses and builders. Certain variables, including sales price (`SLPR`) and floor area (`SQFS`), are top- and bottom-coded, with flags identifying modified cases.

This can distort:

- price-per-square-foot calculations;
- extreme-value analysis;
- correlations and regression relationships;
- luxury-market estimates.

Census explicitly warns that modification alters relationships with other variables. [3]

**Recommendation:** Treat the files as complex-survey data, not independent identically distributed transaction records. Do not assume the public weight alone permits exact design-based uncertainty estimation for every custom statistic.

---

## 10. Quality, uncertainty, and missing information

SOC estimates are subject to both **sampling error** and **nonsampling error**.

Nonsampling risks include coverage omissions, nonresponse, reporting mistakes, coding problems, and imputation. Census publishes standard-error or relative-standard-error information for selected statistics. [4]

### Response rates differ substantially by variable

The methodology reports:

- key dates obtained for approximately **94%** of buildings requiring an interview;
- weighted response rates for most 2025 single-family characteristics of at least **92%**;
- most multifamily-completion characteristics of at least **91%**;
- single-family sales-price response of **65%**;
- contract price, financing type, and lot-size response rates between **64% and 74%**. [4]

These are not interchangeable response metrics.

Census proportionally distributes cases with missing characteristics among cases that reported those characteristics when producing characteristics estimates. Consequently, missingness matters, especially for price and financing analysis.

### Adjustment dependence

Census describes approximate final adjustments of:

- 4% for starts;
- 5% for completions;
- 12% for sales,

to account for relevant prepermit activity and late reports. These are methodological summaries—not fixed correction factors analysts should independently apply. [4]

**Practical rule:** A large-looking month-to-month change can still be statistically indistinguishable from zero. Interpret published uncertainty, revisions, and several months together rather than treating a preliminary headline as an exact count.

---

## 11. Release schedules, revisions, and seasonal adjustment

| Product | Routine revision behavior |
|---|---|
| SOC construction estimates in NRC | Previous two months revised with each preliminary monthly release |
| New-home sales and inventory | Previous three months revised |
| Seasonally adjusted NRC/NRS rates | Previous 63 months revised with April-data releases to update seasonal factors |
| Annual construction estimates | Finalized with February data released in the following year |
| Quarterly products | Separate release and revision schedules depending on subject |

Census also documents exceptional revisions to annual characteristics tables. [4,12]

### Units require attention

A **seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR)** for a monthly flow is the seasonally adjusted monthly estimate multiplied by 12. It is not the actual number of houses built or sold during that month, nor necessarily a forecast of the eventual calendar-year total.

Inventory measures are stocks, not monthly flows. Do not assume every seasonally adjusted statistic is annualized. [5,17]

**For reproducibility, store both the reference period and the release vintage.** Using today’s revised history to backtest a decision made years ago introduces information unavailable at the time.

---

## 12. Typical users and benefits to the public

### Documented users

| User | Documented use |
|---|---|
| Bureau of Economic Analysis | National income and product accounts and GDP development |
| Federal Reserve | Economic conditions and interest-rate effects in housing |
| Council of Economic Advisers | Assessment of economic conditions |
| HUD | Development and evaluation of housing programs |
| Builders and NAHB | Housing demand, construction markets, and product demand |
| Manufacturers | Production schedules and market-share planning |
| Financial institutions | Construction-loan and mortgage demand |
| Insurance companies | Replacement costs and rate adjustment |

Sources: [1,7].

### Public benefits

SOC provides:

- **Economic transparency:** an independent public benchmark for a major interest-sensitive industry.
- **Housing-supply monitoring:** distinguishes proposed construction from projects actually started and completed.
- **Evidence for policy oversight:** helps assess broad construction cycles and housing-program outcomes.
- **Open research access:** people outside industry or government can use the same core statistics.
- **Long historical perspective:** decades of consistent subject coverage support research on booms, recessions, and structural change.
- **Information on what is being built:** characteristics reveal changes in size, design, systems, and construction purpose.

These are benefits of the statistical infrastructure. They should not be interpreted as proof that publishing SOC directly causes lower prices or better housing outcomes.

---

## 13. Value—and limits—for policy advocacy

SOC can support questions such as:

- Is construction moving from authorization to completion more slowly?
- Is new supply shifting between single-family and multifamily housing?
- Are built-for-rent single-family starts changing?
- How are new-home size and heating systems changing?
- Are new-home sales or inventories weakening nationally or regionally?

It cannot, by itself, establish:

- the number of affordable homes available to low-income households;
- neighborhood displacement or racial disparities;
- local zoning-policy effects;
- homelessness or eviction trends;
- all subsidized-housing production;
- net housing-stock growth;
- the environmental footprint of construction.

**Useful complementary sources:** ACS and the American Housing Survey for households and existing housing; BPS and local administrative records for local construction authorizations; HUD program records for assisted housing; the Manufactured Housing Survey for HUD-code homes.

Median new-home sale prices are also **not constant-quality price indexes**: changes can reflect shifts in the location, size, and quality of homes sold.

---

## 14. Preservation and data-library recommendations

### Preserve a collection, not just a spreadsheet

A robust SOC preservation package should include:

1. **Every relevant data distribution**
   - monthly releases;
   - downloadable time series;
   - annual and historical characteristics tables;
   - annual microdata;
   - API snapshots.

2. **Interpretive documentation**
   - variable guides and coded values;
   - questionnaires;
   - definitions;
   - sampling and estimation methods;
   - response-rate and reliability documentation;
   - revision notices;
   - release calendars.

3. **Institutional provenance**
   - OMB control numbers and supporting statements;
   - Federal Register notices;
   - HUD sponsorship documentation;
   - disclosure-review identifiers.

4. **Version evidence**
   - retrieval date and source URL;
   - release date and reference period;
   - preliminary/revised/final status;
   - checksums;
   - original file names;
   - transformation scripts.

### Preserve originals and normalized copies

Keep original XLS/XLSX/PDF/HTML/JSON files. Create CSV or Parquet derivatives for analysis, but preserve:

- workbook sheet names;
- footnotes and table universes;
- cell units;
- missing-value codes;
- category labels;
- disclosure flags;
- date encodings.

A CSV conversion alone can lose crucial metadata.

### Highest-priority preservation risks

- **Files can be replaced at the same URL.**
- Revised time series can erase the originally published estimate unless separately captured.
- Legacy XLS files need durable reading support.
- Questionnaire and variable changes can make apparent trends misleading.
- Old web metadata can misrepresent content currency.
- Geographic identifiers are intentionally limited in microdata; those omissions cannot be repaired by archiving.

No SOC-specific NARA records schedule or guarantee of permanent retention was established in this review. **Public availability today should not be treated as proof of permanent preservation.**

---

## 15. Remaining research gaps

The reviewed evidence did not establish:

- a complete institutional history of SOC’s creation and HUD’s initial sponsorship;
- a verified current total federal program cost or exact HUD/Census funding split;
- a definitive year-by-year inventory of every variable change;
- the final disposition of the 2026 OMB extension proposal;
- a comprehensive retention schedule for public releases and underlying records.

The 2026 notice’s **$0 annual cost to the public** refers to additional reporting expenditures, excluding respondents’ time. It does **not** mean the survey costs government nothing. [6]

This review verified documentation and distribution listings but did **not** conduct a row-level audit of downloaded microdata or test API responses.

## Overall assessment

**SOC is a high-value national statistical resource and a high-priority preservation target.** Its greatest strength is tracking the progression of new private housing from authorization through construction and, for qualifying single-family homes, sale.

Its most consequential limitations are restricted geography, sampling uncertainty, revisions, incomplete coverage of the housing universe, and disclosure-modified single-family public-use files. Responsible use requires preserving definitions, weights, universes, and publication vintages alongside the numbers.

# Survey of Construction: dataset risk assessment

**Assessment date: October 9, 2026**  
**Scope:** Census Bureau’s Survey of Construction (SOC), including New Residential Construction (NRC), New Residential Sales (NRS), annual characteristics tables, and public-use microdata. Agency-wide developments are distinguished from changes specifically affecting SOC.

## Overall assessment

**The strongest documented threat is operational disruption—not deliberate deletion of SOC’s historical data.** Historical resources remain listed, the survey’s OMB clearance is active, and Census proposed extending it **without change** in July 2026. However, the 2025 funding lapse demonstrably interrupted collection and delayed releases. Staffing losses and proposed organizational changes create additional risks.

These rubric ratings are **not numerical probabilities of disappearance**. In particular, the Data Quality rating below reflects a documented loss of **timeliness**, not evidence that published estimates were fabricated or rendered unusable.

**Assessment convention:** I include disruptions documented since January 2025, even where service subsequently recovered. I distinguish a postponed reference period that was later published from a permanently skipped collection or publication.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

| Level | Evidence and assessment |
|---|---|
| **Gone** | Not supported. Historical releases and annual microdata remain listed on Census’s website. |
| **High Risk** | No identified removal of historical SOC data files in the period reviewed. This was not an exhaustive download-and-checksum audit. |
| **Moderate Risk** | Census documents historical changes to categories and tables, including revised price groupings, discontinued PDF distributions, and older reductions in table breakdowns. These are documented product changes, not evidence of a recent purge of historical observations. |
| **No Known Issue** | The microdata page lists **1999–2025** files. NRC retains a historical-release archive. Census also maintains historical characteristics tables and a changes log explaining revisions. |

**Sources:** [SOC microdata](https://www.census.gov/construction/chars/microdata.html); [NRC historical releases](https://www.census.gov/construction/nrc/data/releases.html); [Characteristics summary of changes](https://www.census.gov/construction/chars/historical/changes.html).

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

I found no evidence that historical SOC files or historical observations have recently been withdrawn. Documented statistical revisions and format migrations should not automatically be classified as destructive alteration.

**Preservation caveat:** Historical estimates are not necessarily unchanged. For example, Census recalculated 2020–2022 price tables when introducing new price groupings. Users needing the *originally published* version should preserve release vintages separately.

## 2. Future Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

| Level | Evidence and assessment |
|---|---|
| **Gone** | Not supported. Monthly and annual publication continues. |
| **High Risk** | Census temporarily could not collect construction data during the 2025 shutdown. However, subsequent releases incorporated delayed periods; I found no established permanent omission of a reference month, missed statutory SOC publication deadline, or long-expired ICR. |
| **Moderate Risk** | **Typical publication dates were missed.** October 2025 NRC was released **January 9, 2026**, and October 2025 NRS on **January 13, 2026**—well after their ordinary November release windows. NRC announcements also document combining delayed months into later releases. |
| **No Known Issue** | OMB control **0607-0110** remains approved through **March 31, 2027**. July 2026’s Federal Register notice proposed a three-year extension without change. August 2026 NRC and NRS were published September 17 and September 24, respectively; September releases are scheduled for October 20 and October 27. |

**Sources:** [October 2025 NRC release](https://www.census.gov/construction/nrc/pdf/newresconst_202510.pdf); [October 2025 NRS release](https://www.census.gov/construction/nrs/pdf/newressales_202510.pdf); [NRC announcements](https://www.census.gov/construction/nrc/announcements.html); [July 2026 Federal Register notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-07-20/html/2026-14512.htm); [current schedule](https://www.census.gov/construction/soc/schedule.html).

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

The rubric explicitly places delayed collection or publication at Moderate Risk. That condition occurred, despite subsequent recovery and active clearance.

I am **not** treating backfilled months as permanently skipped publications. Nor does the pending extension imply expired authorization: the current approval remains valid.

## 3. Data Quality

### Evidence by risk level

| Level | Evidence and assessment |
|---|---|
| **Gone** | Not supported; the survey continues. |
| **High Risk** | **Timeliness actually deteriorated** during the shutdown and recovery. Census’s recovery plan states that construction indicators using field representatives could not collect September data during the lapse, and no Census principal economic indicator could collect or process October data during it. |
| **Moderate Risk** | Recovery involved shortening collection windows, compressing review, and reallocating resources. These measures create potential response and review risks, which Census explicitly says it sought to mitigate. Agency-wide staffing problems add an emerging risk. |
| **No Known Issue** | Recent releases retain national/regional estimates, structure-type detail, uncertainty measures, and monthly reference periods. The 2026 SOC extension proposal is “without change”; no permanent SOC reduction in granularity or frequency was identified. |

**Sources:** Census’s [2025 funding-lapse recovery plan](https://www.census.gov/econ/indicators/census-pfei-recovery-2025-lapse-in-funding.pdf); [August 2026 NRC release](https://www.census.gov/construction/nrc/pdf/newresconst_202608.pdf); [SOC methodology](https://www.census.gov/construction/soc/methodology.html); [2026 extension notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-07-20/html/2026-14512.htm).

### Selected level: **High Risk**

This follows the rubric’s literal inclusion of **reductions in timeliness**: the reduction was observed, not merely threatened.

**Important qualification:** This is a rating for the assessment period, not a finding of continuing monthly delays or demonstrated deterioration in numerical accuracy. A strictly *current-condition-only* assessment would more reasonably classify quality as **Moderate Risk**, reflecting residual operational risks after recovery.

## 4. Statutory Context

### Evidence by risk level

| Level | Evidence and assessment |
|---|---|
| **Gone** | Not applicable under this category. |
| **High Risk** | SOC does not have a demonstrated statute prescribing every current table and monthly release deadline. Nevertheless, its authority and programmatic uses are well documented; building permits alone cannot substitute for observed starts, completions, and sales. |
| **Moderate Risk** | A reasonable reading emphasizes that the exact SOC product suite is not expressly mandated by a SOC-specific statute, even though it supports federal housing research and economic policymaking. |
| **No Known Issue** | The collection explicitly cites **13 U.S.C. §§8(b), 131, and 182**, and HUD-related Title 12 authority. Census identifies concrete federal users, including BEA, the Federal Reserve, the Council of Economic Advisers, and HUD. No equivalent substitute for the complete SOC program was identified. |

**Sources:** [Federal Register authority statement](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-07-20/html/2026-14512.htm); [SOC purpose and users](https://www.census.gov/construction/soc/about.html); [SOC methodology and its relationship to permits](https://www.census.gov/construction/soc/methodology.html).

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

Your rubric allows this level where statutory authority is explicitly identified and/or the collection supports implementation of federal programs. SOC has named authority, established federal uses, and distinctive information that permit records do not supply.

**Qualification:** This is **not** a claim that Congress permanently guarantees SOC’s present questionnaires, tables, funding, or release dates. General authorization offers less protection than a detailed publication mandate.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

### Evidence by risk level

| Level | Evidence and assessment |
|---|---|
| **Gone** | Not supported. Census remains funded and SOC continues operating. |
| **High Risk** | Leadership turnover is documented, but Director Robert Santos’s departure was a **resignation**, not a verified dismissal. I did not establish a comparable actual headcount showing at least 1,000 staff lost, a 40% loss, or a 20% enacted budget cut for Census or SOC’s division. |
| **Moderate Risk** | The American Statistical Association’s 2025 assessment estimates Census lost **15% of staffing since FY2024**, satisfying the percentage threshold. NPR independently reported departures of at least five division/office chiefs and hiring constraints. |
| **No Known Issue** | Funding alone is less alarming than the original proposal: enacted FY2026 Current Surveys and Programs funding was **$319 million versus $329 million**, about a **3% nominal reduction**. Total Census funding increased. The FY2026 request for Current Economic Statistics—which includes construction statistics—was unchanged at **$216 million**. |

**Sources:** [ASA Census assessment](https://www.amstat.org/docs/default-source/amstat-documents/the-nations-data-at-risk-2025/census.pdf); [NPR on Census staffing departures](https://www.npr.org/2025/04/17/nx-s1-5349435/us-census-bureau-data-decennial); [CRS FY2026 appropriations analysis](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/IF13105.html); [CRS director history](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF11845); [current Census leadership](https://www.census.gov/about/leadership/director.html).

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

The estimated **15% agency staffing loss** supports Moderate Risk. This is agency-level evidence; SOC-specific staffing losses and the current HUD/Census funding split remain unverified.

The administration proposed reducing the broader Current Surveys account by approximately **12%**, but Congress enacted a much smaller cut. The proposed cut should not be reported as an accomplished reduction.

### What the requested staffing tracker can establish

I examined the [USAJobs Listings Tracker](https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com). It explicitly warns that:

- job listings are **not actual hires**;
- not all federal positions appear on USAJobs;
- collection was to stop **December 31, 2025**.

It therefore cannot establish October 2026 SOC staffing or quantify departures. I did **not** convert vacancy-posting changes into employee-loss percentages.

## 6. Policy

### Evidence by risk level

| Level | Evidence and assessment |
|---|---|
| **Gone** | No SOC termination identified. |
| **High Risk** | No SOC-specific presidential-action-driven ICR, negative policy notice, or implemented administration-directed suppression of SOC outputs was identified. |
| **Moderate Risk** | Broader proposals could affect SOC’s institutional setting: the FY2026 request proposed reorganizing Census, BEA, and BLS and eliminating functions deemed nonstatutory or noncore. A House appropriations proposal would also have limited repeated solicitation of voluntary survey responses; **that provision was not enacted**. |
| **No Known Issue** | The most direct SOC policy evidence favors continuity: Census sought an extension **without change** in July 2026, and Census/HUD continued publishing monthly and annual products. No proposed SOC-specific cancellation or content restriction was found. |

**Sources:** [Census Project analysis of the FY2026 request](https://thecensusproject.org/2025/06/30/department-of-commerce-releases-fiscal-year-2026-census-budget-details/); [CRS on proposed and enacted appropriations provisions](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/IF13105.html); [SOC extension notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-07-20/html/2026-14512.htm).

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

This is an **indirect, agency-policy rating**, based on proposed restructuring and mission-prioritization changes—not evidence that SOC itself has been targeted.

The proposed response-contact restriction was potentially relevant because SOC is voluntary and follows construction projects repeatedly. Its exclusion from enacted legislation substantially reduces that particular threat. The reviewed evidence does not establish final implementation of the broader reorganization.

---

## Preservation implications

**Prioritize protection against interruption and loss of publication versions rather than assuming imminent wholesale deletion.**

Recommended actions:

1. Archive annual microdata, variable guides, characteristics tables, and monthly release PDFs.
2. Capture time-series files and API metadata with retrieval dates and checksums.
3. Preserve both original and revised estimates; routine revisions can overwrite the version used in contemporary decisions.
4. Monitor OMB renewal before **March 31, 2027**, release-date deviations, SOC sample changes, and HUD co-funding.
5. Obtain division-level staffing and budget information before escalating staffing risk to High.

**Evidence limitation:** This review examined official releases, schedules, notices, archives, and contextual reporting. It did not test every historical download or independently audit microdata values.

## Summary of risk levels

Historical Data Availability: **No Known Issue**  
Future Data Availability: **Moderate Risk**  
Data Quality: **High Risk**  
Statutory Context: **No Known Issue**  
Staffing and Funding: **Moderate Risk**  
Policy: **Moderate Risk**
